content: The IUPAC name for beta-alanine is 3-aminopropionic acid. Unlike its counterpart, L-α-alanine, beta-alanine does not possess a chiral center. Beta-alanine is not utilized in the biosynthesis of major proteins or enzymes. It is synthesized in vivo through the degradation of dihydrouracil and carnosine. Beta-alanine is a component of naturally occurring peptides such as carnosine and anserine, as well as pantothenic acid (vitamin B5), which itself is a constituent of coenzyme A. Under normal physiological conditions, beta-alanine is metabolized into acetic acid. Beta-alanine serves as the rate-limiting precursor for carnosine synthesis, meaning that the levels of carnosine are directly dependent on the availability of beta-alanine. Supplementation with beta-alanine has been shown to increase carnosine concentrations in muscle tissue, reduce fatigue in athletes, and enhance total muscular work output. Studies typically employ supplementation protocols involving multiple doses of 400 mg or 800 mg administered at regular intervals over periods ranging from 4 to 10 weeks. Carnosine, a dipeptide composed of beta-alanine and L-histidine, is an important intramuscular buffer. It occurs at concentrations of 17–25 mmol/kg (dry muscle) and contributes 10–20% of the total buffering capacity in type I and type II muscle fibers. Beta-alanine, due to the position of its beta-amino group, is not incorporated into proteins, allowing it to be stored at relatively high concentrations (millimolar levels) in tissues. When ingested in amounts exceeding 10 mg per kg of body weight, beta-alanine can cause paraesthesia (a tingling sensation). This effect varies between individuals. Some may experience mild symptoms at 10 mg/kg, while the majority report significant symptoms at 20 mg/kg, and severe symptoms at 40 mg/kg. However, an equivalent molar amount of beta-alanine ingested in the form of histidine-containing dipeptides, such as carnosine and anserine found in chicken broth extract, does not induce paraesthesia. This is because the absorption profile of beta-alanine from these dipeptides is flattened and sustained over a longer period, unlike the rapid absorption and elimination observed with beta-alanine in powdered form administered via gelatin capsules. In the latter case, plasma concentrations peak within 30–45 minutes and are eliminated within 90–120 minutes. The paraesthesia caused by beta-alanine is not indicative of its efficacy. Published studies have utilized doses of 400 mg or 800 mg at a time to avoid this side effect. Additionally, a significant proportion of beta-alanine (up to 47%) is lost in the urine when administered at doses of 10, 20, or 40 mg per kg body weight, with greater losses occurring at higher dosages. Beta-alanine is a relatively weak agonist for strychnine-sensitive inhibitory glycine receptors (GlyRs) compared to glycine, the primary ligand. The agonist activity hierarchy for these receptors is as follows: glycine >> beta-alanine > taurine >> alanine, L-serine > proline. While beta-alanine is much weaker than glycine, its role as a physiological neurotransmitter remains debated.
